package.description:
On tirzepatide, if you have swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat; problems breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; or a very rapid heartbeat, stop using it and get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Quick answer: where trials counted them, serious risks were uncommon. Severe GI adverse reactions (Zepbound trials): 1.7–3.1% on tirzepatide vs 1.0% on placebo. Thyroid box: C-cell tumors in rats, human risk unknown; not for anyone with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2. NAION: an FDA-flagged potential class-wide eye risk, 6.4 on GLP-1 medicines vs 3.8 on comparators per 100,000 person-years (126 trials, not tirzepatide alone).

Sources:
1. Zepbound PI - https://uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html
2. Zepbound Medication Guide - https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-us-mg.pdf
3. FDA NAION safety communication, 9 Nov 2026 - https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
tags: how rare are mounjaro side effects
package.pinned_comment: The FDA's eye warning (NAION) covers the whole GLP-1 class as a potential risk: 6.4 on these medicines vs 3.8 on comparators per 100,000 person-years, from only 15 probable cases across 126 trials, not tirzepatide alone. The FDA's sign to watch for is sudden, painless vision loss in one eye: contact a healthcare professional right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Save this video for the checklist at your next appointment. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.cta: Subscribe for plain-language reads of the tirzepatide label. Watch-next target for the post notes: Tirzepatide Side Effects. The publisher adds the verified link and leaves line 1 of the description empty. The description must give the full allergy list from the Medication Guide: swelling of face, lips, tongue or throat; problems breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; very rapid heartbeat. For any of these, stop using it and get medical help right away. Don't list depression or suicidal thoughts as a label warning, because the FDA removed it in Jan 2026. Credit the NAION figures (6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years, 126 trials, 15 probable cases, class-wide) to the FDA Drug Safety Communication of 9 Nov 2026, not to the labels. Describe the kidney injury cases as postmarketing reports. The description must end with "Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you." Before publishing: (1) check S2's revision date in the Medication Guide section of the Zepbound listing on DailyMed and replace it with the exact date found; (2) check the live channel list for duplicates.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every number, attribution and safety line against the Zepbound and Mounjaro US prescribing information (both revised 8/2026) and the two FDA Drug Safety Communications (13 Jan 2026 and 9 Nov 2026). All the numbers match their sources:
- severe GI reactions 1.7–3.1% vs 1%
- pancreatitis 0.23 vs 0.11, shown alongside 0.14 vs 0.15
- gallbladder 0.6% vs 0%
- NAION 6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years, from 126 trials with 15 probable cases, class-wide, called a "potential" risk

The indications, including sleep apnea and the Mounjaro heart-event wording, are correct. So are the boxed warning, the contraindications, gastroparesis, kidney injury, low blood sugar in adults without type 2 diabetes, the caution about reactions to another GLP-1 and the removal of the mood warning.

All fixes from the 11-21 hold are in: no repeated NAION number at s65, the sleep apnea card waits for s9, "a sulfonylurea", the full allergy list, "MTC or MEN 2", the wider low-blood-sugar scope and the Medication Guide's own URL. The fixed safety lines are exact.

The Medication Guide PDF exists at its URL, but the tool couldn't extract its text. Its wording was checked against the known Zepbound Medication Guide text instead, and its revision date still needs confirming. That is issue 4 below.

Only minor wording issues remain, each with an exact fix below.

issues.claim: On tirzepatide, your serious risks are real but small in trials, with signs you can spot.
issues.problem: "your serious risks" makes a population result sound personal. Also, several risks in the video (kidney injury, allergic reactions, NAION) come from postmarketing reports or the FDA's class-wide analysis, not from tirzepatide trial rates.
issues.fix: Narration: "On tirzepatide, the serious risks are real, but where the trials counted them they were uncommon, with signs you can spot." On-screen: "Tirzepatide risks: real, uncommon in trials"

issues.claim: The label describes reports of acute kidney injury with this drug class, including Zepbound, sometimes needing dialysis.
issues.problem: The label says these are postmarketing reports. The narration drops that word, so viewers can't tell how this was counted.
issues.fix: "The label describes postmarketing reports of acute kidney injury with this drug class, including Zepbound, sometimes needing dialysis. Most were in people who had lost fluids through stomach and gut side effects."

issues: headline ("which signs matter") is a slightly different angle than the title's rarity question, mild topic drift
"1 IN ?" without a subject could feel slightly abstract at a glance, but "EACH RISK, COUNTED" subtext clarifies it
narrows the video's scope to only the boxed warning, which is a smaller slice of 'serious side effects: how rare' than the title promises
magnifying glass icon is small at phone size

thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates are legible at phone size with a single clear focal point (a simple cartoon face) and none give away the answer or mismatch emotion/text. #1 ("1 IN ?") ties most directly to the title's core question ("How Rare?") with a specific-number curiosity gap that's instantly understandable even at small size, backed by the clarifying "EACH RISK, COUNTED" line. Its shocked-face icon matches the surprising-statistic framing well. #0 is strong too but shifts the angle slightly toward 'which signs to watch for' rather than rarity. #2 narrows the promise to just the boxed warning, which undersells the fuller 'how rare are the risks' scope of the title. #1 best balances curiosity, title alignment, and legibility.
